strengths: Solid theoretical foundation with formal proofs of permutation invariance properties (Lemmas 3.1-3.2, Theorem 3.3); mathematical framework is rigorous and well-presented
Meaningful practical improvements: 2.75× end-to-end speedup in long-context prefilling while maintaining near-full-attention performance on LongBench and LongBench2
Method is orthogonal to existing approaches and composable; demonstrated compatibility with XAttention (Appendix B.2) shows broad applicability
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) and comprehensive appendices containing proofs and implementation details
Commits to reproducibility: uses public models, datasets, benchmarks; detailed experimental setup; commits to releasing code
Addresses a critical real-world problem: computational bottleneck for scaling LLMs to long contexts with important environmental implications
Thorough experimental validation across two different model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B-1M) with multiple strong baselines (Minference, FlexPrefill, XAttention, MeanPooling)
weaknesses: Contribution is somewhat incremental: primarily a clever rearrangement/reordering of attention computation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; core insight that 'permuting sequences can improve sparsity' is relatively straightforward

Limited theoretical motivation: paper doesn't provide quantitative analysis of why keys are 'scattered' before proposing solution; lacks theoretical justification for why query-aware key permutation specifically works
Segmented permutation strategy for maintaining causality (Section 3.2) appears ad-hoc; the interaction between causality preservation and sparsity maximization could be analyzed more rigorously
Applicability is specific to prefilling/inference scenarios and long-context settings; method doesn't address training efficiency, short-context performance, or other inference phases
Code not available at review time, limiting reproducibility verification; custom permuted-FlashAttention kernel lacks detailed implementation specifications
Limited analysis of generalization: only tested on two model families; no systematic study of performance on different architectures, attention patterns, or language domains
Insufficient failure mode analysis: doesn't discuss when permutation strategy might degrade performance or what characteristics of attention patterns make the method effective/ineffective

strengths: Clear problem formulation and motivation: 'Information fragmentation' is well-articulated with formal objective (Eq. 2); Figure 1 convincingly shows global heavy-hitter clustering outperforms local query-key alignment
Solid theoretical foundation: Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and Theorem 3.3 correctly establish permutation invariance properties; segmented permutation elegantly preserves causal masking

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple benchmarks (LongBench, LongBenchv2, RULER), models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B-1M, Qwen3-8B, Qwen-2.5-14B), detailed layer-wise and head-wise analysis showing 70.8% heads benefit/5.2% harmed
Practical engineering: Custom permuted-FlashAttention kernels with manageable overhead (4–5% at scale); GQA handling and detailed timing breakdowns provided
Honest limitations discussion: Section B.5 acknowledges failure modes (diagonal patterns, query-specific attention) with visualizations; doesn't oversell applicability
Well-executed ablations: Systematic studies of segment size, block size, and permutation targets; task-wise proxy sensitivity analysis (Table 4) demonstrates robustness
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: Token permutation for attention is not new (Reformer, concurrent work); core contribution is segmented permutation for causality—a relatively straightforward adaptation of permutation invariance

Performance gaps unacknowledged: LongBench shows 37.37 vs. 38.28 (−0.91 points); RULER at 128K shows 66.98 vs. 75.30 (−7.3 points); paper claims 'closely match full attention' despite these non-negligible gaps; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Context-dependent efficiency: Speedup <1.2× at 8K–16K contexts where permutation overhead dominates (74.6% overhead at 4K); method impractical for shorter sequences; limited applicability

Weak baseline: MeanPooling is introduced in this paper, not previously established; compared baselines (FlexPrefill, Minference) show significant accuracy drops, confounding attribution of gains to selection vs. permutation; XAttention comparison limited to appendix

Proxy scoring under-analyzed: Using last-block queries as global importance proxy is ad-hoc; Figure 1 shows marginal differences across proxy strategies, suggesting robustness may hide poor proxy quality; no analysis of why last-block specifically or generalization to diverse patterns

Unresolved failure modes: 5.2% heads harmed by permutation; diagonal 'slash line' patterns fundamentally incompatible; acknowledged but unaddressed ('pruning strategies left for future work'); limits practical applicability

Limited scope: Evaluation on decoder-only LLMs only; focus on prefilling—decoding patterns may differ; H100-only evaluation limits generalizability; no analysis of interaction with positional embeddings (RoPE, ALiBi)

Reproducibility limitations: Code unavailable despite '(available at)' claim; GQA replication mechanism unclear; hyperparameter choices (B=128, S=256) presented as fixed without full sensitivity analysis
